antenna-001.question: What is the electrical length (a half wavelength, ignoring end shortening) of a half-wave dipole antenna used at 150 MHz? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
antenna-001.explanation: The wavelength is λ = c/f = 3×10⁸/(150×10⁶) = 2 m, and half of that, 1 m, is the electrical length of a half-wave dipole. 2 m is one full wavelength, and 0.5 m is λ/4, the length of a monopole (whip antenna) mounted over the ground or a ground plane. In a real dipole, the conductor thickness and end effects shift the resonance slightly lower in frequency, so the total length is cut a few percent shorter than a half wavelength to make it resonate. This shortening depends on the conductor thickness and is not the same thing as the velocity factor of a coaxial cable.

antenna-002.question: Which is closest to the feed-point radiation resistance of a half-wave dipole made of thin wire and placed in free space?
antenna-002.explanation: The theoretical radiation resistance of a thin half-wave dipole is about 73 Ω, with a slightly inductive reactance (about +j42 Ω). That is why, in practice, it is made a few percent shorter than a half wavelength to bring it to resonance. About 36.5 Ω is the value for a λ/4 monopole over a perfectly conducting ground, which is half that of the dipole when the image is included. About 300 Ω is the value for a folded dipole (about 292 Ω, roughly four times 73 Ω), which has been used because it matches 300 Ω twin-lead feeder easily. When feeding from 50 Ω coaxial cable, consider both matching and balanced-to-unbalanced conversion (a balun).

antenna-003.question: What is the gain in dBi of an antenna with a gain of 10 dBd (take the gain of a half-wave dipole as 2.15 dBi)?
choices: 10 dBi (the same value regardless of reference)
antenna-003.explanation: dBi is gain relative to an isotropic antenna (a hypothetical antenna radiating uniformly in all directions), and dBd is gain relative to a half-wave dipole. A half-wave dipole has 2.15 dB more gain than an isotropic antenna, so dBi = dBd + 2.15, giving 10 + 2.15 = 12.15 dBi. 7.85 dBi subtracts in the wrong direction. The references differ, so the numbers are not the same. When comparing gains in datasheets, check which reference is used, or you will miss a difference of about 2 dB.

antenna-004.question: Which correctly describes the relationship between antenna gain and directivity?
choices: A high-gain antenna amplifies the fed power through the resonance of its elements before radiating it, so its gain exceeds its directivity
Gain and directivity are always equal; conductor and dielectric losses do not affect gain and only change the input impedance
Gain is directivity multiplied by radiation efficiency, so it is less than the directivity when there is loss inside the antenna
antenna-004.explanation: Directivity D compares how concentrated the radiated power is in a given direction with an isotropic antenna. Gain G is referenced to the power fed into the antenna, and is expressed as G = ηD using the radiation efficiency η, which includes conductor and dielectric losses. For example, with D = 10 dBi and 50% efficiency, G ≈ 7 dBi. An antenna is a passive device and cannot increase power; its gain is high because it gathers power into a particular direction while weakening other directions. G = D holds only in the ideal case of 100% efficiency.

antenna-005.question: Which is closest to the effective aperture of an antenna with 20 dBi gain (100 as a linear value) used at 3 GHz (a wavelength of 0.1 m)?
antenna-005.explanation: The effective aperture is Ae = Gλ²/(4π); with G = 100 and λ = 0.1 m, Ae = 100 × 0.01/(4π) ≈ 0.0796 m², about 0.080 m². About 1.0 m² forgets to divide by 4π, and about 0.016 m² puts the dB value 20 directly into the formula, which needs the linear value. For the same gain, the shorter the wavelength, the smaller the aperture; conversely, for an antenna of the same size, the higher the frequency, the higher the gain. For a parabolic dish, Ae is the physical aperture area multiplied by the aperture efficiency.

antenna-006.question: Which is closest to the free-space path loss at 1 GHz over a distance of 10 km? Take the free-space path loss as L = 20 log₁₀(4πd/λ) dB and the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
antenna-006.explanation: λ = c/f = 0.3 m, so 4πd/λ = 4π × 10⁴/0.3 ≈ 4.19×10⁵, and L = 20 log₁₀(4.19×10⁵) ≈ 112.4 dB. The commonly used form L = 32.45 + 20 log₁₀ f(MHz) + 20 log₁₀ d(km) gives the same result, 32.45 + 60 + 20 ≈ 112.4 dB. About 92 dB is an order-of-magnitude error that takes the distance as 1 km. About 56 dB uses 10 log; free-space path loss is the square of (4πd/λ), so 20 log is used. This loss comes from the wave spreading out spherically; the energy is not absorbed by space.

antenna-007.question: In free space, how much does the received power change when the distance between transmitter and receiver is doubled (with the same antennas and frequency)?
antenna-007.explanation: In free space the power density is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, so doubling the distance cuts the received power to 1/4, a drop of 20 log₁₀ 2 ≈ 6 dB. Ten times the distance gives 20 dB. About 3 dB wrongly assumes the power falls in proportion to distance, to 1/2. About 12 dB (1/16) is the case for a radar echo, where the round trip makes the fourth power of distance matter; it does not apply to one-way communication. In the flat-earth two-ray model, where the ground-reflected wave interferes with the direct wave, the power can fall off closer to the fourth power at long range, but that is not free space.

antenna-008.question: When the polarization directions of linearly polarized transmit and receive antennas differ by 60°, what is the polarization mismatch loss (all other conditions equal)?
antenna-008.explanation: The receivable power is proportional to cos²θ for a polarization angle difference θ; at θ = 60°, cos²60° = 0.25, a loss of 10 log₁₀(1/0.25) ≈ 6.0 dB. About 3 dB treats cos θ = 0.5 as a power ratio; the electric-field component is multiplied by cos θ, so the power goes as its square. About 1.2 dB is cos²30° = 0.75 (10 log₁₀(1/0.75) ≈ 1.25 dB), from measuring the angle the wrong way. At 90° nothing is received in theory, and this property is used for polarization frequency reuse, sending different signals on vertical and horizontal polarizations at the same frequency.

antenna-009.question: Which statement about circular polarization is correct?
choices: Receiving circular polarization with a linearly polarized antenna picks up only one of its two orthogonal components, so the loss is about 3 dB regardless of orientation
Receiving right-hand circular polarization with a left-hand circularly polarized antenna costs only about 3 dB, because they share a linear component
In circular polarization the direction of the electric field stays fixed and only its magnitude rises and falls sinusoidally
antenna-009.explanation: In circular polarization the electric-field vector rotates at constant magnitude; it can be viewed as the sum of two orthogonal linear polarizations 90° out of phase. A linearly polarized antenna receives only one of these components, so it gets half the power, a loss of about 3 dB, regardless of orientation. Circular polarizations with opposite senses of rotation (right-hand and left-hand) are orthogonal, so in theory almost nothing is received. A field whose direction stays fixed while only its magnitude varies is linear polarization. Circular polarization is used in satellite communications and GNSS because it is less affected by Faraday rotation in the ionosphere and by polarization misalignment due to antenna orientation.

antenna-010.question: Both ends of a link use parabolic antennas with a fixed effective aperture, and the frequency is doubled with the distance and transmit power unchanged. What happens to the received power in free space?
antenna-010.explanation: Substituting G = 4πAe/λ² into the Friis transmission equation Pr = Pt·Gt·Gr·(λ/4πd)² gives Pr = Pt·At·Ar/(λ²d²). With fixed apertures, the received power is proportional to 1/λ², that is, to the square of the frequency, so doubling the frequency increases it fourfold (about 6 dB). A decrease of about 6 dB applies to antennas of fixed gain (dipoles, for example), where only the increase in free-space path loss matters. The saying "the higher the frequency, the greater the path loss" assumes fixed-gain antennas; with fixed aperture, the opposite holds.

antenna-011.question: On a 10 km line-of-sight link at 6 GHz (a wavelength of 0.05 m), which is closest to the radius of the first Fresnel zone at the midpoint (5 km from each end)? Take the first Fresnel zone radius as r = √(λd1d2/(d1 + d2)).
antenna-011.explanation: With d1 = d2 = 5000 m and d1 + d2 = 10000 m, r = √(0.05 × 5000 × 5000/10000) = √125 ≈ 11.2 m. The radius is largest at the midpoint and shrinks toward the ends. About 16 m is √(λd1) = √250 ≈ 15.8 m, dropping the factor d2/(d1 + d2). About 35 m is an order-of-magnitude error that takes the wavelength as 0.5 m (600 MHz). Even if the straight line of sight is clear, ground or buildings inside the Fresnel zone increase loss through diffraction and reflection, so on fixed microwave links the antenna heights are chosen with Fresnel zone clearance in mind.

antenna-012.question: The tip of a thin, plate-like obstacle (a knife edge) just touches the line of sight between the transmit and receive antennas. Which is closest to the theoretically known diffraction loss in this case?
choices: 0 dB (the line of sight is clear, so there is no loss)
antenna-012.explanation: In knife-edge diffraction theory, when the tip of the obstacle just touches the line of sight, the field at the receiver is about half its free-space value, a power loss of about 6 dB. Even with the straight line of sight unobstructed, the wave propagates with the spread of the Fresnel zone, and half of it is blocked, so the loss is not zero. The loss grows as the obstacle rises above the line of sight; about 20 dB corresponds to the tip protruding about 1.7 times the first Fresnel zone radius above the line of sight (a diffraction parameter v ≈ 2.4). Conversely, when the obstacle is well below the line of sight, the loss approaches 0 dB.

antenna-013.question: With the same radar, when the range to the same target (with the same radar cross section) doubles, what happens to the received echo power?
antenna-013.explanation: In the radar equation, the received power is Pr = Pt·G²·λ²·σ/((4π)³R⁴), inversely proportional to the fourth power of the range R. The transmitted wave weakens by 1/R² on the way to the target, and the wave scattered by the target weakens by another 1/R² on the way back. Doubling the range gives 2⁴ = 16, so 1/16, a drop of about 12 dB. 1/4 wrongly uses the square of the range, as in one-way communication, and 1/8 uses the cube. To double the maximum detection range with everything else equal, the transmit power must be increased 16 times; this R⁴ dependence is what makes radar design so demanding.

antenna-014.question: When the diameter of a parabolic antenna is doubled (with the same frequency and aperture efficiency), how do its gain and beamwidth change?
choices: The gain increases by about 6 dB, and the beamwidth roughly halves
The gain rises by about 3 dB, and the beamwidth is about 1/√2
The gain rises by about 6 dB, but the beamwidth does not change
antenna-014.explanation: Gain is proportional to the aperture area (G = 4πAe/λ²); doubling the diameter quadruples the area, so the gain rises by about 6 dB. Beamwidth is roughly proportional to λ/D, so doubling the diameter nearly halves it. About 3 dB wrongly treats the gain as proportional to the diameter rather than the area. Higher gain concentrates the power into a narrower direction, so the beamwidth cannot stay the same. Gain and beamwidth are two sides of the same coin; the sharper the beam, the more accurately the antenna must be pointed.

antenna-015.question: A parabolic antenna 1 m in diameter is measured at 10 GHz (a wavelength of 0.03 m). Which is closest to the Fraunhofer distance 2D²/λ, the usual guideline for the far field?
antenna-015.explanation: 2D²/λ = 2 × 1²/0.03 ≈ 66.7 m, about 67 m. Closer than this, the phase errors caused by differences in distance from each part of the antenna to the measurement point (more than π/8) can no longer be ignored, and the far-field radiation pattern and gain cannot be measured correctly. About 33 m forgets the factor of 2, and about 6.7 m is an order-of-magnitude error that takes the wavelength as 0.3 m (1 GHz). The larger the aperture and the higher the frequency, the longer this distance becomes, so large antennas are evaluated in compact ranges or with near-field measurements and transformed to the far field by calculation.

antenna-016.question: A short dipole has length l equal to 1/20 of a wavelength (l = λ/20). If the current can be taken as uniform along its whole length, the radiation resistance is Rr = 80π²(l/λ)². Which is closest to this radiation resistance?
antenna-016.explanation: Substituting l/λ = 0.05 gives Rr = 80π² × 0.05² = 80 × 9.87 × 0.0025 ≈ 1.97 Ω, about 2.0 Ω. About 39 Ω forgets to square (l/λ), and about 7.9 Ω uses twice the length, λ/10. Because radiation resistance is proportional to the square of the length, it drops quickly for antennas shorter than a wavelength. With a triangular current distribution that goes to zero at the tips, as in a real short dipole, it is a further 1/4 of this value. If the conductor loss resistance is 2 Ω, the radiation efficiency Rr/(Rr + Rloss) falls to about 50%, and the input reactance is strongly capacitive, so handling loss and matching is central to the design of short antennas.

antenna-017.question: Which statement about the unfed elements (reflector and directors) of a Yagi–Uda antenna is correct?
choices: The reflector is made slightly longer than the driven element and the directors slightly shorter, and the wave is radiated strongly toward the directors
The reflector is made slightly shorter than the driven element and the directors slightly longer, and the wave is radiated strongly toward the directors
The reflector and directors are the same length as the driven element and are driven in phase by current split from the feed line, strengthening both forward and backward directions
antenna-017.explanation: Only the driven element (a half-wave dipole) is fed; the other elements are parasitic, picking up the driven element's wave and reradiating it. A reflector slightly longer than a half wavelength is inductive and a director slightly shorter is capacitive, and the difference in the phase of their induced currents makes the reradiated waves add on the director side and cancel on the reflector side. If the length relationship is reversed, the longer elements act as reflectors, so the wave does not head toward the elements called directors. Feeding the elements and driving them in phase is the idea of an array antenna. Adding directors raises the gain, but with diminishing returns, and the feed-point impedance falls below 73 Ω, so a folded dipole or similar is used for matching.

antenna-018.question: Which correctly describes what happens when a balanced half-wave dipole is fed directly by an unbalanced coaxial cable without a balun?
choices: Because the coaxial cable is shielded by its outer conductor, current flows only inside, with no effect on the radiation pattern or the feed-point impedance
Unbalanced current flows on the outside of the outer conductor, so the cable itself radiates and distorts the pattern, and the feed-point impedance changes
Current flows in only one arm of the dipole, so the radiation resistance halves to about 36.5 Ω and the gain drops by exactly 3 dB
antenna-018.explanation: Equal and opposite currents flow on the inner conductor and on the inner surface of the outer conductor of a coaxial cable. When it is connected to a dipole, part of the current heading to the arm on the outer-conductor side flows back onto the outer surface of the outer conductor. This current flows along the cable and radiates by itself, distorting the pattern, and the currents in the two arms become unbalanced, which also changes the feed-point impedance. The shield works only for current flowing on the inside of the outer conductor. Current does flow in both arms, so the impedance does not become about 36.5 Ω, which is the value for a λ/4 monopole over ground. A balun converts between balanced and unbalanced and suppresses this outside current (common-mode current).

antenna-019.question: Without changing the frequency, an antenna is made much smaller than a wavelength (ka ≪ 1 for the radius a of the smallest sphere enclosing it, with k = 2π/λ). Which correctly describes what happens?
choices: The smaller it gets, the higher its radiation resistance becomes and the easier it is to match to 50 Ω, so the usable bandwidth actually widens and the gain rises
With a cleverly designed matching network, bandwidth and efficiency can be kept regardless of size, so the limit on miniaturization is set only by manufacturing accuracy
The lower bound on the radiation Q rises roughly as 1/(ka)³, so the bandwidth that can be matched narrows, and efficiency also tends to fall because of losses
antenna-019.explanation: A small antenna has a lot of nonradiating stored energy around it, so its Q, the ratio of that energy to the radiated power, is large. According to the Chu limit, the lower bound on the Q of an antenna that fits in a sphere of radius a is about 1/(ka)³ + 1/(ka), which for ka ≪ 1 rises in inverse proportion to the cube of the size. Since the fractional bandwidth is roughly proportional to 1/Q, halving the size cuts the upper limit on bandwidth to about 1/8. The radiation resistance also becomes small, so efficiency falls relative to the loss resistance of the conductors and matching components. A matching network can cancel the reactance at a particular frequency, but it cannot exceed this bandwidth limit. Saying that the radiation resistance rises is backward.

antenna-020.question: An antenna has a main-beam half-power beamwidth of 20° in each of two orthogonal planes. If the directivity is estimated as D ≈ 41253/(θ1·θ2), where θ1 and θ2 are the half-power beamwidths in the two planes in degrees, which is closest?
antenna-020.explanation: 41253/(20 × 20) = 41253/400 ≈ 103, and 10 log₁₀ 103 ≈ 20.1 dBi, about 20 dBi. 41253 is the full solid angle of 4π sr converted to square degrees (4π × (180/π)²), and the approximation assumes the power is spread uniformly over the region bounded by the half-power beamwidths. About 30 dBi is 41253/40 ≈ 1031, from adding the beamwidths instead of multiplying them, and about 40 dBi converts the ratio 103 to dB with 20 log, which is wrong because directivity is a power ratio and takes 10 log. Real antennas also leak power into sidelobes, so this approximation overestimates the directivity, and the gain is that directivity multiplied by the radiation efficiency.
